tagline.text: The Mariveles monument where the 1942 Death March began

location.label: Location
location.text: Along a main road in downtown Mariveles, Bataan (confirm the exact spot locally)

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: November–May dry season, around Araw ng Kagitingan on April 9

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱800–1,500 (day trip from Manila including round-trip transport, per person)

children.text: The Death March Km 0 marker in Mariveles is a white obelisk marking one of the points where prisoners began walking to Capas after the Battle of Bataan ended in April 1942. It is in downtown Mariveles at the southern tip of the Bataan Peninsula, so it fits well into a trip combined with Corregidor and Mount Mariveles.

The Death March Km 0 marker is a white obelisk standing in downtown Mariveles at the southern tip of the Bataan Peninsula. It marks one of the starting points of the "Bataan Death March," in which American and Filipino prisoners had to walk toward Camp O'Donnell in Capas after Bataan fell to Japanese forces in April 1942. A Km 0 marker with the same name also stands in Bagac, so the starting points are described as two: Mariveles and Bagac. One account says the group that set out from Mariveles began on April 10, 1942.

The marker is less a large memorial hall than a small roadside memorial park. The white obelisk carries the Filipino phrase "Pinagsimulan ng Death March," meaning the beginning of the Death March, along with a bilingual historical plaque. One visitor describes a nearby metal sculpture in the form of a soldier's grave, with an M1903 rifle and a World War I-style helmet represented, symbolizing the defenders of Bataan. The plaque is said to have been donated by the Filipino-American Memorial Endowment (FAME) and the American Chamber of Commerce of the Philippines.

The Death March began right after the Battle of Bataan ended on April 9, 1942. The state broadcaster PTV reports that more than 70,000 Filipino and American prisoners were forced to make the march, and thousands died from beatings, shootings, bayonetting and beheading as well as starvation and disease. The route ran on foot from Mariveles and Bagac to San Fernando, Pampanga, then by train to Capas and again on foot to Camp O'Donnell, and the total distance is given as about 140 km to 160 km depending on the source. Death tolls also differ greatly by source, so it is best to treat them as estimates. More people are said to have died of hunger and disease after reaching Camp O'Donnell.

The marker itself can be seen in a short visit. One travel guide gives the visiting time as 15–30 minutes, but if you also tour nearby war sites, plan 1–2 hours. If you are interested in Bataan's war history, continue from Mariveles to the Mount Samat Shrine, the Philippine-Japan Friendship Tower in Bagac and Corregidor. Exact placement and the surroundings can change, so check before you go. Mariveles is a port town at the southern end of the Bataan Peninsula, and one visitor says they rented a banca to Corregidor from here.

The white obelisk by the road is the first of the kilometer markers set up along the Death March route. The markers show the distance walked, are all painted white and are said to have been built with donations. This one is zero, and the numbers increase along the route.
A historical plaque in Filipino and English announces the start of the march. It says this is where the Death March began, and the obelisk is said to carry the words "Pinagsimulan ng Death March."

The memorial park is said to have a metal sculpture representing an M1903 rifle and a helmet. One visitor describes it as the form of a soldier's grave. It is a symbol honoring the defenders who fought in Bataan.

About 138 markers are said to stand along the route from Mariveles and Bagac to the Capas National Shrine. Counts differ by source: about 97–100 in Bataan, about 31–33 in Pampanga and 7–8 in Tarlac. Some are described as damaged or missing. Markers mentioned by name include KM 6 and KM 21 in Bataan, KM 35 in Orion and KM 58 in Orani. Most stand along the national road, so take care for your safety beside the traffic.

April 9 each year is the Philippines' Araw ng Kagitingan (Day of Valor). Philippine Veterans Week events are held around then, and PTV has reported on the 82nd commemoration. If you want a quiet visit, it is best to avoid this period.
Corregidor Island, which guides say is about
15 minutes

by boat from Mariveles harbor, is described as the place where US forces surrendered on May 6, 1942. You can follow the story of how the island was isolated and fell after Bataan collapsed. One historical account says Japanese General Homma expected the Bataan campaign to take 50 days, but it actually lasted about 120 days. Corregidor's Malinta Tunnel served as MacArthur's headquarters and a 1,000-bed hospital, and more than 4,000 people are said to have worked there during the battle.

blocks.title: Link to the Capas National Shrine

children.text: The Capas National Shrine in Tarlac, the end point of the march, is said to have the final marker. Seen together with this Km 0 marker, you will have visited both the beginning and the end.

items.title: A half day in Mariveles
items.subtitle: The monument and the harbor area

children.text: Take a bus bound for Mariveles from Pasay or Cubao in Manila. Guides say it takes 3–4 hours.
Arrive in downtown Mariveles. The marker is beside a main street, reachable by tricycle or on foot.
See the Km 0 obelisk and the plaque, and look around the soldier's grave sculpture. There is no shade, so wear a hat.
Head to the harbor area and look out toward Corregidor Island. If you have time, look into a Corregidor tour.
Have lunch in town.
Return by bus bound for Manila or Balanga. Confirm the last Manila bus time locally.
Rather than seeing only the marker, combining it with other Bataan war sites into a full day gives more value for the travel time.

items.title: A day of Bataan war sites
items.subtitle: From Mariveles to Bagac and Mount Samat

children.text: Start with the Km 0 marker in Mariveles.
Move toward Bagac and look for the Philippine-Japan Friendship Tower and the Km 0 marker in Bagac.
Have lunch in Bagac or Balanga.
Go up to the Mount Samat Shrine to see the cross and the museum.
Head to Balanga to stay overnight, or return to Manila.
You need to hire a vehicle to combine several sites in one day. Public transport alone may not leave enough time.
Take a Genesis or Bataan Transit bus bound for Mariveles from Cubao or Pasay. The fare is given as about
for a trip of 3–4 hours (varies by operator and terminal; no official fare table, so confirm locally).
Mariveles is the free port town at the southern tip of the Bataan Peninsula, reached by going down Roman Highway from Layac Junction.
Guides say the last bus to Manila leaves around 7 to 7:30 p.m., but it varies by operator and terminal, so confirm your return time in advance.
In Mariveles town, take a jeepney or tricycle to the marker. The fare depends on distance and bargaining.
The marker is close to the road, so it may not be quiet because of passing traffic.
Take NLEX and SCTEX, then follow Roman Superhighway into Mariveles town.
Parking in front of the marker may be limited, so use a lot in town.
Search a map app for "Death March Zero Kilometer" and then confirm the exact spot locally. Sources describe it differently, as in front of the municipal hall or along a downtown road.
The marker is an outdoor site open 24 hours a day, so there are no time limits, but there is no shade and it is hot by day. One guide names January to March as the best period.

Ceremonies are held on April 9, Araw ng Kagitingan, and during Philippine Veterans Week in early April, so it is crowded. If you want to visit on a meaningful day this is the time, but expect crowds. Araw ng Kagitingan is a public holiday in the Philippines, so transport may be crowded and some facilities may be closed, so allow plenty of time.
In the June–October rainy season there are rains and typhoons, and the area around the marker can be muddy. To avoid the midday sun, early morning or late afternoon is better.

Mariveles is a port town at the southern end of the Bataan Peninsula, so there is little lodging. If your schedule runs late, you can use small guesthouses in Mariveles or Balanga town. If you need to stay overnight, Balanga has more choices.

One visitor report says there is a Jollibee right next to the marker, so a simple meal is easy. In town there are restaurants serving Filipino home cooking and market food. Visitors also say trash has piled up around the banca landing at the harbor, so decide on a seaside meal after seeing local conditions.

If you plan to spend a night in Bataan, a realistic plan is to base yourself at a hotel in Balanga and visit Mariveles, Bagac and Mount Samat in turn. Restaurants in Mariveles town may close early, so eat dinner early before moving on.
The site is beside a road, so watch for vehicles when crossing.
There is almost no shade, so bring a hat, sunscreen and water.
You will get much more from the visit if you read the plaque. Read an overview of the Battle of Bataan and the Death March before you leave.
The marker is a short stop, so build your itinerary around it with Corregidor, Mount Samat and Mount Mariveles.
Some markers are said to be damaged or missing, so a plan to find every marker is unrealistic.
Around April 9 the area can be crowded with commemorations, so arrive early.
When taking photos, observe the respect appropriate to a memorial site.
On a day trip from Manila, be sure to check the last bus time.
Guides say the Bataan tourism office is inside the provincial capitol compound in Balanga and takes inquiries on weekdays from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m.
The exact location of the marker and its surroundings are described differently by different sources. Check the location on a map before you go, and ask locals once more on site.
It is beside a road, so traffic noise is loud and you need to take care as a pedestrian.
There is no shade, so it is very hot at midday.
Sources differ on dates (March 10 or April 10) and on death tolls, so do not insist on a single figure.
At a memorial site, avoid loud voices and inappropriate behavior.
Set your return time in advance so you do not miss the last bus to Manila.

A shrine built on the site of Camp O'Donnell, the end point of the Death March.
